clinicalPearls: Caused by usually de novo variants in GNB1, which encodes the beta1 subunit of heterotrimeric G-proteins that relay signals from G-protein-coupled receptors to downstream effectors including ion channels
Core features are developmental delay and intellectual disability with hypotonia, and epilepsy occurs in a substantial subset
Seizures, when present, are variable in type, including focal, generalised, and infantile spasms, and range from readily controlled to drug-resistant
A movement disorder can occur, with dystonia or other involuntary movements, overlapping the broader G-protein-related phenotypes
Additional features may include feeding difficulties, growth problems, visual impairment, and, in some, a predisposition to certain haematological abnormalities

Because the beta subunit modulates effectors such as G-protein-gated potassium channels, disease reflects disturbed signalling rather than a single channel defect, and antiseizure therapy is broad-spectrum and empirical
GNB1 shares mechanistic ground with GNAO1 as a heterotrimeric G-protein subunit disorder, though the phenotypes differ
reference.pathophysiology: GNB1 encodes the beta1 subunit of heterotrimeric G-proteins, which together with gamma subunits transmits signals from activated G-protein-coupled receptors to effectors including adenylate cyclase, phospholipase C, and G-protein-gated inwardly rectifying potassium channels. The beta-gamma complex is essential for correct assembly and signalling of the G-protein cycle. Pathogenic variants disrupt subunit interactions and downstream signalling, perturbing neuronal excitability and neurotransmission across many circuits. This broad signalling disturbance produces the combination of intellectual disability, hypotonia, epilepsy, and movement disorder, and because the defect is upstream of multiple effectors, treatment cannot target a single channel.
additionalDifferentials: Other genetic causes of intellectual disability with epilepsy and movement disorder
additionalInvestigations: Gene panel or whole-exome sequencing to identify the GNB1 variant
Electroencephalography where seizures are present, to characterise type
Brain magnetic resonance imaging to exclude structural causes
Haematological review if blood-count abnormalities are noted
redFlags: Infantile spasms or drug-resistant seizures with developmental regression
Significant feeding failure or unexplained haematological abnormality
reference.prognosis: Most affected individuals have intellectual disability of variable severity with hypotonia; seizures and movement disorder, when present, add to the burden, and cognitive outcome is generally guarded though heterogeneous.
pitfalls: Excluding the diagnosis because it is a signalling protein rather than an ion channel
Overlooking the associated movement disorder or haematological features
Conflating the phenotype with GNAO1 despite differing clinical patterns
Expecting a channel-specific therapy to be available
references: GeneReviews and OMIM resources on GNB1-related neurodevelopmental disorder
ILAE resources on genetic developmental and epileptic encephalopathies
management: Treat seizures with broad-spectrum antiseizure medication chosen empirically, as the defect lies upstream of multiple effectors rather than a single channel
Manage dystonia and other involuntary movements with movement-disorder pharmacotherapy
Provide developmental and rehabilitative support with physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language therapy
Address feeding difficulties and poor growth with nutritional support or gastrostomy, and manage visual impairment
Monitor for and treat associated haematological abnormalities
Coordinate multidisciplinary neurology, epileptology and developmental paediatrics, and offer genetic counselling given usually de novo variants
